candidato.titulo: STAT+: Pharmalittle: We’re reading about a cancer vaccine, an experimental pancreatic cancer drug, and more
candidato.resumo: A personalized mRNA cancer vaccine reduced the risk of disease recurrence in patients with melanoma by 42% compared to a standard treatment

texto_fonte:
And so, another working week will soon draw to a close. Not a moment too soon, yes? This is, you may recall, our treasured signal to daydream about weekend plans. Our agenda is, so far, rather modest. We plan to manicure the Pharmalot grounds, catch up with some folks who have been hiding, and promenade with the official mascots. We also expect to hold another listening party, where the rotation will likely include this, this, this, this and this. And what about you? As we have previously noted, this is the time of year when the Great Pumpkin is growing lonely, so perhaps you have time to stop by a patch to say hello. If that fails, you can always visit an orchard or simply hike about. Or if the weather fails to cooperate, a moving picture show may be in order. You could also plan the rest of your life, which may be a good idea before AI does it for you. Well, whatever you do, have a grand time. But be safe. Enjoy, and see you soon. …
A large clinical trial testing a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine reduced the risk of disease recurrence in patients with melanoma by 42% compared to a standard treatment, STAT tells us. The results are an important advance because patients lived significantly longer without cancer returning. The vaccine may also usher in a new wave of treatments for other types of cancer, though experts are debating how broadly applicable the technology could be. Merck and Moderna announced its success in August, but details including the magnitude of benefit were being withheld until a scheduled presentation Saturday at the annual meeting of the European Society of Medical Oncology. But an oncology news website published some of the data on Thursday, breaking the conference embargo.
A U.S. judge granted a request by the Pharmaceutical Research & Manufacturers of America and three drug makers to intervene in a lawsuit over a government rebate pilot program, pivoting from a previous decision denying their involvement, Bloomberg Law notes. The order will allow the trade group, AbbVie, Bristol Myers Squibb, and Boehringer Ingelheim to step into a fresh legal battle over the 340B Rebate Model Pilot Program slated to go into effect Jan. 1. Hospitals filed a challenge earlier this month seeking to block the U.S. Health Resources & Services Administration from allowing drugmakers to provide rebates instead of upfront discounts for medicines purchased through the 340B Drug Discount Program.

candidato.titulo: A quick squeeze helps CRISPR turn skin cells into neurons more efficiently
candidato.resumo: Human cells hold about two meters (6.6 feet) of DNA, folded and compacted to fit inside a nucleus. That packing is essential for life, but it creates a problem for scientists. Some of the genes that control a cell's identity are buried so deep in tightly packed DNA that gene-targeting tools such as CRISPR activation, or CRISPRa, struggle to reach them.

texto_fonte:
A quick squeeze helps CRISPR turn skin cells into neurons more efficiently
Human cells hold about two meters (6.6 feet) of DNA, folded and compacted to fit inside a nucleus. That packing is essential for life, but it creates a problem for scientists. Some of the genes that control a cell's identity are buried so deep in tightly packed DNA that gene-targeting tools such as CRISPR activation, or CRISPRa, struggle to reach them.
That problem lies at the heart of cell reprogramming, which converts one type of cell into another. Scientists can turn a patient's skin cells into neurons, heart cells or other hard-to-obtain cell types to study how a disease develops, test drugs for safety and effectiveness, and potentially grow replacement tissue the patient's immune system is less likely to reject. But the process remains stubbornly inefficient. In mouse cells, often only a few percent of cells convert, and in human cells, the success rate can fall to a fraction of a percent.
Now, UCLA researchers have found a physical way to improve those odds. In a study published in Matter, the team describes a strategy that squeezes the nucleus for just milliseconds, temporarily loosening tightly packed DNA so CRISPRa can reach and switch on genes it would otherwise struggle to access.
In mouse cells, the approach raised the share of skin cells that became neurons from about 3% with CRISPRa alone to about 40%. The biggest gains came when the squeeze was used as a priming step that made the cells more adaptable.
"Even when the reprogramming factors are inside the cell, the last mile of the problem is that they can't get access to the sites they need to bind to activate genes," said senior author Song Li, associate dean for graduate and professional education and a professor of bioengineering at the UCLA Samueli School of Engineering and a member of the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center. "We are addressing that last-mile problem, which is accessibility."
Why genes get locked away
Nearly every cell in the body carries the same genome, yet a neuron looks and behaves nothing like a skin cell. The difference is in the epigenome, the layer of chemical and structural controls that decides which genes are open for use and which are shut. Li compares it to a computer: The genome sequence is the hardware, and the epigenome is the operating system that determines what the machine actually does.
Genes a cell doesn't need are packed away tightly in dense chromatin—the DNA and protein packaging inside the nucleus. A neuronal gene in a skin cell isn't normally used, so it's often stored this way.
That locked-away DNA is also hard for gene-targeting tools like CRISPRa to reach. Unlike conventional CRISPR gene editing, CRISPRa activates genes without cutting the DNA sequence. A short piece of RNA guides the tool to its target, but finding guides that work efficiently often requires trial and error.
Mapping where the squeeze opens DNA
In earlier work, the Li lab showed that briefly squeezing the nucleus of skin cells loosened DNA packaging and improved reprogramming. This study builds on that discovery by identifying precisely which regions of the genome become more accessible after squeezing and using that information to guide CRISPRa.
By combining genome-wide mapping with targeted gene activation, the researchers developed a strategy that not only makes DNA easier to access but also helps CRISPR tools find more effective sites for switching on genes that control cell identity.
"CRISPRa is very site-specific," said Li, who is also a member of the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center and the California NanoSystems Institute at UCLA. "With the map in hand, we can design and guide RNAs to target those open sites."
Turning skin cells into neurons more efficiently
The team first delivered CRISPRa and its guide RNAs to adult mouse skin cells as short-lived RNA instead of using a virus, a common alternative that can raise safety concerns. Because the tool can't cut DNA, the cells' genes could be switched on without being permanently altered. A day later, the cells were passed through a microfluidic chip, a device with channels narrower than the cell nuclei, which briefly squeezed and deformed them.
The approach, called mechanically enhanced CRISPR-mediated activation, or MECA, affected many genes, including Ascl1 and Brn2, which can steer a skin cell toward becoming a neuron. The squeeze made those genes far more active, and the effect was strongest when the guides were aimed at spots the squeeze had opened. About 10% of skin cells became neurons, compared with about 3% with CRISPRa alone.
On its own, the squeeze doesn't change a cell's identity. It opens a window in which CRISPRa can do that work more easily.
"It's like giving the cell some exercise, so it has more plasticity," Li said.
Next, the team used the same approach to switch on Oct4, a gene that helps stem cells stay flexible enough to become many cell types. With the squeeze, far more skin cells switched on Oct4, moving partway toward a stem cell–like state without fully becoming stem cells. More of them were dividing, and their DNA was less tightly packed.
That priming paid off. When the researchers then switched on Ascl1 and Brn2 in these cells, about 40% became neurons, far more than with the squeeze and CRISPRa alone.
Beyond this study
MECA isn't tied to one way of getting CRISPRa into cells. Because it tackles a separate problem, how accessible the DNA is within cell nuclei, it could be paired with different delivery approaches. And this method gives researchers a rational way to choose targets: the spots in the genome that become reachable after the squeeze.
The team now plans to test whether the approach works for other kinds of human cell conversions and whether the resulting cells function well enough for uses like drug testing and transplantation.
The researchers also found that activating Oct4 with this approach made skin cells from aged mice appear biologically younger, based on DNA chemical patterns that scientists use to estimate age. Several other signs of cellular aging improved as well. The results suggest that mechanical gene regulation could be useful for studying how cells age and how that process might be reversed.
These findings add to growing evidence that physical forces shape how our genomes behave.
"Cells in our body feel physical forces every second, from the stretch of a muscle to the load on a bone, just as they respond to chemical signals," Li said. "So this should be studied together with the chemical and biological factors."
Publication details
Yang Song et al., Mechano-epigenetic enhancement of CRISPR activation of target genes for cell reprogramming, Matter (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.matt.2026.103064

candidato.titulo: Robôs e IA começam a transformar o futuro da exploração espacial
candidato.resumo: A inteligência artificial já ajuda robôs a explorar Marte de forma autônoma. O que vem pela frente? Saiba tudo no Olhar Espacial O post Robôs e IA começam a transformar o futuro da exploração espacial apareceu primeiro em Olhar Digital .

texto_fonte:
Em dezembro do ano passado, um robô percorreu parte da superfície de Marte seguindo uma rota planejada por inteligência artificial (IA). O rover Perseverance, da NASA, realizou dois deslocamentos com trajetos definidos por IA, em uma demonstração que aponta para um futuro em que máquinas poderão explorar outros mundos com maior independência.
O episódio representa um avanço significativo – até então, a definição das rotas do veículo dependia do trabalho de especialistas na Terra. Com a nova tecnologia, a IA analisou imagens e informações sobre o terreno para identificar obstáculos e propor caminhos seguros.
A mudança responde a um dos principais desafios das missões espaciais: a distância. Os sinais entre a Terra e Marte levam vários minutos para percorrer o espaço, o que impede o controle dos veículos em tempo real. Quanto maior a autonomia dos robôs, menor a necessidade de esperar por novas instruções.
Outra iniciativa que ajuda a entender esse caminho é o projeto Exploração Robótica Distribuída, Autônoma e Cooperativa (CADRE, na sigla em inglês), da NASA. A proposta envolve pequenos robôs que trabalham de forma coordenada na Lua, compartilhando informações e explorando o terreno em conjunto. Mas como máquinas diferentes podem cooperar em um ambiente tão imprevisível quanto o espaço?
Os exemplos também levantam dúvidas sobre os limites dessa autonomia. Como garantir que um sistema tome decisões seguras diante de situações inesperadas? Qual deve ser o papel dos especialistas humanos quando os robôs passam a escolher seus próprios caminhos? E até onde a IA pode transformar a maneira como exploramos o Sistema Solar?
Essas são algumas das questões que estarão em pauta no programa Olhar Espacial desta sexta-feira (23), que recebe Roberto ‘Pena’ Spinelli, físico graduado pela Universidade de São Paulo (USP), com especialização em Machine Learning pela Universidade de Stanford, nos EUA, pesquisador na área de IA e colunista do Olhar Digital News, para um bate-papo sobre como a inteligência artificial e a robótica podem transformar os rumos da exploração espacial.
Como assistir ao Programa Olhar Espacial
Apresentado por Marcelo Zurita, presidente da Associação Paraibana de Astronomia – APA; membro da SAB – Sociedade Astronômica Brasileira; diretor técnico da Rede Brasileira de Observação de Meteoros (Bramon) e coordenador nacional do Asteroid Day Brasil, o programa é transmitido ao vivo, todas as sextas-feiras, às 21h (horário de Brasília), pelos canais oficiais do veículo no YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, X (antigo Twitter), LinkedIn e TikTok. Mas atenção! Excepcionalmente desta vez, o programa começa mais cedo, às 20h20!

candidato.titulo: AWS Introduces Lambda Web Functions for Node.js Applications
candidato.resumo: AWS recently introduced Lambda Web Functions, allowing developers to run Node.js web applications using frameworks such as Express and Hono directly on Lambda, with support for concurrent requests and response streaming. By Renato Losio

texto_fonte:
AWS recently introduced Lambda Web Functions, allowing developers to run Node.js web applications using frameworks such as Express and Hono directly on Lambda, with support for concurrent requests and response streaming.
According to the Lambda Web Functions documentation, the new functions support concurrent HTTP requests and response streaming. They charge for active CPU time and memory, rather than CPU time spent waiting for downstream services. Multi-Region routing directs requests to the closest Region, while a single warm execution environment can handle multiple concurrent requests, significantly reducing cold starts. Existing Lambda functions are now called Lambda Event Functions, with no changes required. Micah Walter, senior solutions architect at AWS, summarizes the benefits and why it removes this complexity:
You can take a standard port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or any Node.js framework, deploy it with a single command, and Lambda automatically handles scaling, multi-region distribution, and active CPU billing. No adapters, no infrastructure to manage, and no framework lock-in.
Endpoints use a Lambda-provided domain by default. To use a custom domain, edge caching, or AWS WAF, developers can use Amazon CloudFront in front, relying on Lambda Web Functions as the origin.
Lambda Web Functions target HTTP workloads, including full-stack web applications, REST and GraphQL APIs, and independently scaling microservices. They also support server-side rendering and streaming responses, such as incremental output from large language models, without requiring a separate hosting layer.
Lambda Web Functions currently support only Node.js; other languages, including Python, Java, and .NET, remain available through traditional Lambda functions. Earlier this year, AWS also launched Lambda MicroVMs, which provide isolated, stateful sandbox environments for running untrusted or user-generated code, with customer-managed lifecycles.
In their article "Exploring AWS Lambda Web Functions for Building Web Applications", Julian Wood, Kim Wendt, and Samrat Karak build a sample application to show how one execution environment handles many requests at once and how the application serves users globally. They summarize:
Lambda Web Functions bring the serverless operating model to web applications without adapter layers. You write a standard Node.js HTTP server, deploy it with one command or CloudFormation, and get a scalable, pay-per-use HTTPS endpoint with global routing built in.
Community reactions on Reddit and Hacker News have been largely positive, highlighting the simpler programming model and support for concurrent requests. However, discussions also raise questions about Python support and how the service differs from existing alternatives. User magnetik79 comments:
This is a big one - and nice to see something not entirely honed in AI. ☺️ What looks great: Many workloads can now skip API Gateway entirely (...) this totally changes the current Lambda HTTP programming model - now you're no longer working with one invoke/one request - now you might need to be sync/mutex aware.
In his article "Why I'm Excited About AWS Lambda Web Functions," Eric Johnson, principal developer advocate at AWS, highlights how Lambda Web Functions run standard HTTP servers and frameworks without modification, supporting REST, server-sent events, streaming responses, RPC, webhooks, and IAM authentication through a single managed endpoint.
AWS is not the only cloud provider offering this model: Google Cloud Run and Azure Container Apps also support web applications without adapter layers, scale-to-zero, and configurable concurrency, making them suitable for workloads with intermittent or bursty traffic.
Pricing for Lambda Web Functions is based on active CPU time and memory usage, potentially reducing costs for workloads that spend time waiting on databases or APIs. Memory is billed for the lifetime of the execution environment. This model may benefit I/O-heavy workloads, such as server-side rendering, API backends, and streaming AI inference. The service is currently available in five regions: Northern Virginia, Ohio, Oregon, Tokyo, and Ireland.

texto_fonte:
AMD desmente teoria sobre relançamento do Ryzen 7 5800X3D; entenda real motivo
Por Raphael Giannotti |
O primeiro processador considerado rei dos games é o Ryzen 7 5800X3D, lançado em 2022 e trazendo grande desempenho por conta da implementação da tecnologia 3D V-Cache. Quatro anos depois, essa mesma CPU retorna ao mercado, mas esse relançamento é um "presente final" de Lisa Su, CEO da AMD, à grande base de usuários da plataforma AM4.
Quem disse isso foi Travis Kirsch, um dos diretores da AMD, em entrevista no Japão. Questionado sobre o motivo pelo qual levou ao relançamento desse processador nesse ano, o executivo disse que "de um ponto de vista de fabricação, a produção do Ryzen 7 5800X3D original acabou", e o mesmo não era mais fabricado, mas Lisa Su trouxe a ideia de relançar essa CPU anos atrás como um presente para os usuários.
"Originalmente, há vários anos, creio que a Lisa foi uma das pessoas que sugeriu relançar o Ryzen 7 5800X3D. Foi como um presente final para nossos usuários fiéis, que utilizaram nossa plataforma AM4 por quase 10 anos, dando a eles uma última chance de atualizar seus PCs com sistemas DDR4", disse Kirsch.
Decisão aconteceu antes da atual crise
Ele deixa claro que isso foi decidido "antes das mudanças que aconteceram no mercado de memórias e não foi considerado como uma solução à escassez de DDR5". Ou seja, o timing foi perfeito, para dizer o mínimo, já que na metade de 2026, quando a crise já estava muito severa, a AMD traz novamente o primeiro rei dos games ao mercado.
Infelizmente, o novo modelo, que é chamado de "Edição de aniversário de 10 anos do AM4", chegou consideravelmente mais caro, com preço ajustado à realidade atual do mercado. Para se ter uma noção, o Ryzen 7 5800X3D hoje custa o equivalente a um Ryzen 7 9800X3D, que é o melhor processador para games hoje.
Claro, existe a diferença da plataforma. Para quem está no AM4 há anos, faz muito sentido adquirir um 5800X3D, que será a melhor opção disponível hoje, já que os Ryzen 9 da série 5000 estão escassos no mercado hoje. Assim, é possível ter um ótimo desempenho em termos de CPU sem a necessidade de migrar para AM5 e encarar os preços absurdos das memórias DDR5.

candidato.titulo: Webb image reveals young stars brewing in a nebulous cauldron
candidato.resumo: In this Picture of the Month from the NASA/ESA James Webb Space Telescope, we visit a turbulent cauldron of star formation to see what is brewing inside dense clumps of gas. This is a star-forming region named LHA 120-N 159, or simply N159, located 161,000 light-years away in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), one of the satellite galaxies orbiting the Milky Way galaxy. This image spans about 230 light-years across.

texto_fonte:
Webb image reveals young stars brewing in a nebulous cauldron
In this Picture of the Month from the NASA/ESA James Webb Space Telescope, we visit a turbulent cauldron of star formation to see what is brewing inside dense clumps of gas. This is a star-forming region named LHA 120-N 159, or simply N159, located 161,000 light-years away in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), one of the satellite galaxies orbiting the Milky Way galaxy. This image spans about 230 light-years across.
N159 is what astronomers call an H II region: an area of space filled with ionized hydrogen gas. In stellar nurseries such as this one, giant molecular clouds of cold hydrogen gas collapse under gravity, forming new stars. Many of these stars are extremely massive and hot, and their powerful ultraviolet radiation ionizes the gas around them. This makes H II regions markers of active star formation, and as the ionized gas radiates light, this turns them into the kind of brilliant emission nebula that we see in this image.
The fierce stellar winds from these stars sculpt dense ridges and carve open cavities in the gas, which Webb's Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) captures here in great detail.
The roiling brew of star formation in N159 is closed in by thick, smoky orange clouds that also billow across the center of the image. The light orange color signifies light emitted by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, important carbon-based molecules. The pools of pale blue gas are clouds of H II gas, ionized by the intense ultraviolet light from massive stars.
Dark red filaments cross the center of the image, particularly visible above the blue region on the right side; these are made of cool molecular hydrogen. These filaments are the densest part of the nebula and currently shield new stars from harsh radiation and stellar winds—by zooming in, you can see stars as points of light embedded in these filaments and in the small pillars of orange gas that reach out into the blue bubbles. Eventually, these structures will melt away, leaving their completed stars behind.
The LMC is full of H II regions like N159 conveniently located for us to study, including the larger N79 region and the spectacular Tarantula Nebula. They are not exactly like the star-forming regions within our own galaxy: The LMC's metallicity—its proportion of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium, which astronomers call "metals"—is significantly lower than in the Milky Way galaxy. This gives researchers an opportunity to study H II regions in conditions that are more similar to those found in the early universe, helping us to learn about star formation in that time.
At less than 3 million years old, N159 is one of the youngest star-forming regions of the LMC, containing thousands of stars at their earliest stages of formation. Since the advent of space telescopes, astronomers have closely examined the stellar populations in N159. The brightly glowing spot on the left side of the image is the Papillon Nebula, an exceptionally compact blob of ionized hydrogen that is thought to be linked to the formation of massive stars: It was resolved for the first time by the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope in 1999.
Sections of the sweeping clouds of gas were featured in a pair of images from Hubble in 2025, covering the east and west sides of the cloud.
The data used in this new Webb image come from an observing program (#5114) aiming to study and compare stars throughout their different stages of evolution in this giant nebula. In the resulting paper posted to the arXiv preprint server, astronomers delved into N159 in greater detail thanks to these new and comprehensive Webb data. They were able to detect extremely dim stars less than a tenth as massive as the sun, and distinguish larger, hotter, fully evolved stars from the young stellar objects still wrapped up in the thick clouds where they are born.
Their results showed that the western region of N159 has more of these young stellar objects in a more concentrated area, showing that it is at an earlier stage of collapsing to form stars. With the whole sequence of star formation taking place at once, N159 is a unique place to see the evolution of a collapsing molecular cloud up close.
Publication details
Nolan Habel et al., Sequential Star-Formation and the Near-Infrared Stellar Populations within N159, arXiv (2026). DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2609.27126

candidato.titulo: IQM and Telefónica Plan Quantum Computer for Madrid University
candidato.resumo: Insider Brief PRESS RELEASE — Telefónica and IQM Quantum Computers, a global leader in superconducting quantum computing, have joined forces to deploy the first quantum computer in the Community of Madrid. The initiative will strengthen the region’s scientific and technological capabilities, while driving the development of real-world cases for companies across the Community of Madrid. […]

texto_fonte:
Insider Brief
- Telefónica and IQM Quantum Computers plan to install the first quantum computer in Spain’s Community of Madrid at the Technical University of Madrid (UPM) before the end of 2026.
- The IQM Spark system is designed for research, education and early-stage development, giving universities, hospitals, research centers and start-ups access to quantum hardware.
- The project aims to build regional expertise, support the development of industry use cases and expand Madrid’s role in Europe’s quantum technology ecosystem.
PRESS RELEASE — Telefónica and IQM Quantum Computers, a global leader in superconducting quantum computing, have joined forces to deploy the first quantum computer in the Community of Madrid. The initiative will strengthen the region’s scientific and technological capabilities, while driving the development of real-world cases for companies across the Community of Madrid.
The IQM Spark quantum computer, an all-in-one solution specifically designed for research, education and early-stage development, will be installed at the Technical University of Madrid (UPM) before the end of 2026. It will enable universities, hospitals, research centers and start-ups, direct access to real quantum hardware to develop and test quantum algorithms and build the expertise needed to explore future use cases.
This will be the first quantum computer of its kind in the Community of Madrid, significantly increasing the region’s capacity to develop quantum capabilities locally and through hands-on experience. The computer will join the other two quantum computers provided by Telefónica and IQM to CESGA (Galician Supercomputing Centre).
Once the new quantum computer is operational, the Community of Madrid will have greater capabilities to foster the creation of its own quantum ecosystem, bringing together all stakeholders involved in developing real-world use cases that deliver direct benefits to local industry. This ecosystem will help attract talent and strengthen Madrid’s position as a leading hub for advanced digital innovation, while also contributing to the development of European technological sovereignty.
Borja Ochoa, non-executive Chairman of Telefónica España and CEO of B2B, said: “This project marks another step forward in Telefónica’s close collaboration with the Community of Madrid in the deployment of quantum technologies, both in networks and in the encryption and protection of critical data in particularly sensitive sectors such as healthcare and security, and now also through the research opportunities offered by quantum computing. In line with its goal of becoming the best gateway to digital technologies for citizens, businesses and public administrations, Telefónica is the first operator in Spain to offer communications between data centers protected by the new post-quantum cryptography standards. Our company is also helping to build a national ecosystem by developing technologies and communications, specialized centers and strategic projects ranging from the development of cancer treatments to reducing the use of cardboard by packaging companies”.
Jan Goetz, CEO and Co-founder of IQM Quantum Computers, said: “By investing in its own quantum computer, the Community of Madrid is creating an infrastructure that will enable its researchers, students and industries to grow their capabilities over the long term. Quantum computing becomes truly valuable when it moves beyond remote laboratory environments and is placed directly in the hands of those working closest to the real-world challenges it can help address. This deal represents an important step forward for Madrid and for Europe in its ambition to lead the development of quantum computing”.
This project further expands IQM’s growing international footprint, with full-stack quantum computers already deployed across Europe, Asia and North America, including computers supplied to some of the world´s leading supercomputing centers. IQM is also driving the adoption of quantum computing in areas such as research, materials science, financial modelling and other fields, by giving end users direct ownership of the infrastructure needed to turn experimentation into real-world, high-impact applications.
Mohib Ur Rehman
Get the latest research, company news, and market intelligence every week.
MENTIONED IN THE ARTICLE
Telefónica specializes in telecommunications and digital services, operating fixed, mobile, broadband, and digital platforms across Europe and Latin America. In the quantum domain, the company focuses on quantum communications, quantum-safe security, and post-quantum cryptography to address future cybersecurity risks to telecom networks. Through its innovation arm Telefónica Innovación Digital and Telefónica Tech, it develops and pilots quantum-resilient security solutions in collaboration with technology partners, research institutions, and European programs to enable secure communications for enterprises and critical infrastructure.
IQM Finland builds scalable hardware for universal quantum computers, focusing on superconducting technology.

texto_fonte:
It takes a lot to live up to a $7,000 price tag. Asus’ ProArt P16 RTX Spark certainly does when it comes to the hardware. With 128GB of memory, a spectacular 16-inch OLED display, and a remarkably thin and rigid all-metal chassis, it feels like a serious Windows challenger to Apple’s premium MacBook Pros despite a couple of annoying quirks. It’s utterly stunning hardware, full stop.
I’m working on a full review of this beautiful monster, centered on the reason it exists in the first place: Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip, a monumental memory pool, and what happens when you stop paying the cloud to run enormous AI workloads and start doing them locally instead. RTX Spark laptops are an entirely new class of Arm-based Windows machines, with models from Microsoft, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo, culminating with this ProArt’s eye-watering $7,000 price tag.
My testing is deep, weird, and still underway. Stay tuned.
But that review is going to spend a lot of time talking about CUDA cores, tokens, local AI models, and benchmarks. Before disappearing down that rabbit hole, I want to talk about the actual laptop—because this feels like a premium machine designed to brawl with high-end MacBook Pros.
The Asus ProArt P16 is the cleanest, most imposing laptop I’ve ever reviewed. It reminds me of Darth Vader in the best possible way: a big, cold, imposing black slab of metal that looks like it means business. Real “You may dispense with the pleasantries, Commander. I am here to put you back on schedule” kinda vibes. That’s exactly what I want from a $7,000 laptop.
Better yet, Asus somehow squeezes its 16-inch display and 128GB of unified memory in a chassis just 0.51 inches thick and 3.95 pounds. It feels almost impossibly thin when you pick it up, yet the metal construction is rigid as a carbonite-frozen Han Solo, without flex or creaking. The hinge opens smoothly with one hand. The black finish looks fantastic, though it picks up fingerprints and oils over time. That may simply be because I’m a fat greasy degenerate gamer, but hey, on the plus side it also proves easy to wipe away.
More surprising: This thing usually stays remarkably quiet in many (but not all) scenarios. I’ve spent hours hammering large local AI models while developing my real-world benchmark suite, and the P16 remained far less audibly intrusive than I expected from hardware this potent and thin. I haven’t tried gaming on it though.
An OLED fit for $7,000
The 16-inch OLED touchscreen is just as luxurious. Its 3840×2400 resolution and 283 pixels per inch make everything razor sharp, while the 120Hz refresh rate keeps motion smooth. OLED’s perfect blacks and punchy contrast make colorful images almost seem to loom over the panel rather than exist inside it. It’s bright, dense, vibrant, and gorgeous. Seriously — I’ve never touched a laptop with an OLED panel this luxurious and delightful, even if it doesn’t translate well to static pictures.
Brad Chacos/Foundry
The glossy finish is much less luxurious outdoors. Reflections make the P16 difficult to use in bright sunlight, and there’s another interesting quirk: When direct sunlight hits the screen at the right angle, the touch and pen layer becomes startlingly visible, breaking parts of the display into a fine rainbow-like pattern that I could easily capture on camera (though the effect was more striking in person than it is in photos). Notebookcheck also noticed graininess from the touchscreen layer in its independent testing. It’s essentially invisible during my normal indoor use, but once you see it blazing away in direct sunlight, you can’t unsee it. Hell, you can’t see around it!
The display comes with another futuristic trick that I quickly disabled. Windows Hello uses presence sensing to automatically lock the laptop when you walk away and dim the display when you stop looking at it.
Unfortunately, I stare at my keyboard while I type and think. While I was building a local AI project, the ProArt repeatedly decided I had stopped paying attention and dimmed the display, then brightened it again when I looked up at my output. The resulting flickering drove me nuts. If you stare at your screen while typing, your mileage may vary. I turned it off despite loving the concept in theory.
Wait, where did my RAM go?
The ProArt P16’s 128GB of LPDDR5X memory also behaves unlike RAM in any conventional Windows laptop I’ve used.
Brad Chacos/Foundry
Open Windows and you may wonder why your $7000, 128GB laptop says it has only around 64GB of system memory. RTX Spark uses unified memory shared between its Grace CPU and Blackwell GPU, and that pool can be partitioned between conventional system RAM and memory reserved for the GPU. My machine initially exposed roughly half of its 128GB to each.
Developers accustomed to unified-memory workstations may shrug. Coming from standard Windows laptops with discrete GPUs, I certainly didn’t. More importantly, that enormous configurable memory pool is central to RTX Spark’s pitch: It lets the GPU tackle AI models that simply can’t fit into the dedicated VRAM on normal laptop graphics chips. I’ll dig much deeper into that in the full review.
Brad Chacos/Foundry
Elsewhere, Asus put the P16’s space to excellent use. The six-speaker sound system kicks ass, delivering breadth and actual bass in a way you rarely hear from notebook speakers. Run the Jewels and Zack de la Rocha’s “Close Your Eyes (And Count to F***)”—my unofficial bass torture test—absolutely slaps on this thing. It sounds good enough to make me reconsider my usual “just put on a gaming headset” maxim. (Fun aside: It sounds awesome on Apple’s $699 MacBook Neo, too.)
I wish the webcam received the same attention. A basic 1080p IR webcam is fine, I guess, but this is a $7,000 machine designed for serious professional work. At this price, give me 4K so I look my best on Teams calls.
Fortunately, Asus didn’t skimp on connectivity. It crammed three 40Gbps USB4 ports, USB-A, HDMI, a headphone jack, and a full-size SD Express 7.0 card reader into this remarkably thin chassis. Serious work often means moving significant amounts of data onto and off your laptop. Having this much high-speed connectivity built in feels genuinely luxurious, and it’s a perfect fit for a creator-focused laptop like the ProArt 16.
A great keyboard with a serious problem
My feelings about the keyboard and glorious Death Star-sized haptic touchpad are much more complicated.
Brad Chacos/Foundry
Most of the keyboard is excellent. The keys feel responsive and the layout makes sense, though I’ll always prefer a mechanical keyboard for hours of serious typing. Likewise, I was thrilled when I saw that gigantic touchpad. Give me room to swipe around a 2400p display!
But the touchpad reaches right underneath the spacebar, and my thumb naturally rests along the bottom edge of the spacebar while I type. I found myself repeatedly brushing the touchpad, causing the cursor to teleport elsewhere in my document and dump words into random sentences. Remember: I look at my keyboard while typing, so sometimes I don’t discover the carnage immediately. Changing how I hit the spacebar helps, but forces me to hover my hand farther over it, which starts hurting my wrist over time.
Brad Chacos/Foundry
Worse, the spacebar itself frequently fails to register my presses. I see words smashed together at least once per sentence. It’s maddening.
Interestingly, Dave James at PC Gamer encountered a different keyboard problem with his ProArt P16, reporting occasional unwanted repeated keystrokes rather than my missed spaces. Two reviewers experiencing different keyboard problems isn’t evidence of a systemic defect, but it’s enough to make me suspicious that something funky may be happening here.
Brad Chacos/Foundry
I also wish Asus included a numpad, which I almost never say about laptops. Believe me, I understand the tradeoff. Those excellent upward-firing speakers occupy the space. But engineers and developers buying a $7,000 professional workstation tend to, you know, type lots of numbers.
Battery life has been encouraging during light use, too. While browsing the web and working in documents, Windows initially projected nearly 14 hours away from the wall. Treat that strictly as an observation rather than a benchmark; I haven’t run PCWorld’s formal battery test yet, and hammering local AI models is obviously another matter entirely.
The important part is what happens under the hood with RTX Spark
Brad Chacos/Foundry
My early performance experience otherwise broadly tracks what my colleague Mark Hachman found in his full review of Microsoft’s RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra: middling single-core CPU performance, much stronger multicore performance, and outstanding RTX-class graphics capabilities from Nvidia’s unusual Arm-based SoC. Mark spent over a week pushing RTX Spark through a battery of tests, including local AI workloads.
But conventional benchmarks aren’t the question I really want this $7,000 Asus ProArt P16 to answer.
I want to know what happens when you take complicated work that normally burns through expensive cloud AI tokens and move it onto your laptop. I’m building an intensive real-world AI benchmark around an actual research workload to find out—not merely measuring how quickly RTX Spark spits out tokens, but how much useful work a huge local model can perform, where it falls down, and what happens when you combine local and frontier AI rather than treating them as rivals.
Asus nailed the physical object, maddening spacebar and all. This is the single most impressive laptop hardware I’ve ever had the fortune to touch. The full review will determine whether RTX Spark makes this beautiful monster worth $7,000.

texto_fonte:
1Password cria forma de liberar login sem dar a senha para IAs; veja como funciona
Por André Lourenti Magalhães • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
O 1Password lançou uma nova solução para liberar as senhas de cada pessoa de forma segura durante o uso de agentes de IA. O gerenciador consegue preencher as credenciais automaticamente, mas não informa nenhuma senha ou dado sensível para o serviço de inteligência artificial.
De acordo com a empresa, o 1Password for Agents (“1Password para Agentes”, em tradução livre) é uma forma de garantir que os clientes usem as ferramentas mais avançadas de IA sem perder o controle sobre os próprios dados. O recurso é compatível com bots de Meta, Claude, OpenAI, Perplexity e outras empresas do mercado.
Um agente de IA pode pedir acesso a uma conta de aplicativo para concluir uma tarefa automatizada, mas a medida exige login com senha e até autenticação em dois fatores. A nova solução permite liberar o acesso sem deixar as credenciais sob controle dos bots.
Como o 1Password funciona com agentes de IA
Ao chegar a uma tela de cadastro, o agente usa uma chave digital para verificar a identidade com o 1Password e envia um pedido com as credenciais necessárias para completar o login (senha ou código de verificação, por exemplo).
O gerenciador de senhas comunica o usuário sobre o pedido, informa de onde veio e qual o motivo do acesso, e depois libera para a pessoa permitir ou não o acesso. Com a aprovação, o aplicativo preenche a senha no formulário sem enviar as informações para o agente.
Assim, o login é finalizado de forma segura e o servidor de IA não tem acesso às credenciais do indivíduo. O recurso está disponível para contas individuais e familiares das assinaturas pagas do 1Password.

candidato.titulo: Data-driven operation of biogas plants: Generating electricity when wind and solar power are scarce
candidato.resumo: Biogas plants are considered the third pillar of renewable electricity generation in Germany. Unlike solar and wind power, electricity generation from biogas is largely independent of weather conditions and can generally be scheduled.

texto_fonte:
Data-driven operation of biogas plants: Generating electricity when wind and solar power are scarce
Biogas plants are considered the third pillar of renewable electricity generation in Germany. Unlike solar and wind power, electricity generation from biogas is largely independent of weather conditions and can generally be scheduled.
With an amendment to the Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG) planned for 2027, the regulatory framework is expected to place greater emphasis on flexible, market-oriented electricity generation: Biogas plants would supply electricity primarily when solar and wind generation is low. To support this shift, the number of operating hours eligible for remuneration is expected to be limited.
For operators of the nearly 10,000 biogas plants currently operating in Germany, the timing when electricity is fed into the grid from combined heat and power (CHP) units will increasingly determine the economic viability of their operations. Expanding gas storage capacity is likely to be economically viable for only some older plants.
Fraunhofer IGB has developed a cost-effective digital approach to electricity-price-based operation: An "Edge Device" is connected to the existing plant control system, consolidates process and operational data, and makes these data available onsite for models and AI applications—without requiring changes to the existing control logic.
Biogas plants generate more data than they use
A biogas plant generates a significant amount of data: Sensors measure temperatures in the digester, the composition of the biogas and the fill level of the gas storage tank.
The plant control system tracks the rotational speeds, runtimes and operating statuses of pumps and agitators. It also logs warnings and malfunctions. Other information is not measured directly but is equally crucial—such as which substrates are fed into the system and in what quantities.
However, the majority of this information is used solely for the immediate operation of the plant. "For long-term analyses, forecasts or comprehensive optimization, the data are often not available in the required format," explains Alexander Laug, a process engineer at Fraunhofer IGB.
Measured values are often stored only for a limited time, data structures vary, and important contextual information—such as operating states or threshold values—is available only separately.
Optimizing the operation of a biogas plant requires the various data sets to be considered together. A temperature reading of "40 degrees," for example, only gains meaning within the context of the plant: In which tank was it measured, and what setpoint applies there? Is the associated pump running, and is the plant in automatic or manual mode? Which substrates were added previously, and how is gas production developing?
A data platform in the control cabinet
The Edge Device brings these data together. "Our Edge Device is an industrial computer that is installed onsite. It adds a data processing and computing layer to the existing programmable logic controller (PLC)," explains Laug.
The Edge Device retrieves process and operational data from the PLC, stores them over extended periods and organizes them in a consistent structure. This creates a common data foundation that links current measurements, historical trends and associated operating states. External information, such as electricity price forecasts and weather forecasts, can also be integrated.
Data processing takes place directly onsite. "Operational data do not necessarily have to be transferred to an external cloud," Laug explains. Instead, operators decide for themselves which data leave the plant and which are processed exclusively locally. In doing so, Fraunhofer IGB relies on a technical architecture that is as open as possible. This allows the platform to be adapted to different plants and tasks and expanded with additional models or applications.
The Edge Device bridges conventional plant automation and data-driven plant operation. While the PLC remains responsible for reliable plant control, the Edge Device adds data storage, analytics and computing capabilities for forecasting, optimization and AI models. Multiple applications can build on the same data foundation. These may include electricity price and gas production forecasts, soft sensors, energy optimization and predictive maintenance.
From data to decisions
The real added value arises when the aggregated data are transformed into concrete operational recommendations. The system takes into account not only the plant's current status but also how it has evolved over time.
"It can determine how gas production and gas composition have changed following the addition of a specific feedstock, how full the gas storage tank is, or how long pumps and other equipment have been running," explains Laug. Not every application needs to intervene directly in the plant control system. Models can initially focus solely on analyzing data and generating recommendations for operational staff.
Generating electricity when it delivers the greatest value
For electricity-price-based operation, the data platform combines the current plant status with electricity price forecasts. "A high expected electricity price alone is not enough to make a decision—sufficient gas must also be available, and the plant must be technically capable of operating as planned," says Laug.
Accordingly, the system considers expected gas production, the gas storage level, available combined heat and power (CHP) capacity, and technical operating constraints. Based on these inputs, the model proposes an operating schedule: When should biogas be stored? When should the CHP unit run? And when is electricity generation likely to yield the highest revenue at forecast market prices?
Feedstock also influences electricity generation
Digital optimization can begin even earlier in the process, because the amount of biogas available at a given time depends largely on the feedstock supplied to the digester. Substrates differ in their organic content, biogas yield potential and cost. They also produce biogas at different rates.
By combining these data with historical operating data, it becomes possible to assess how a particular substrate mix affects subsequent gas production and, in turn, electricity generation.
"An optimization model can calculate how an available substrate mix should be composed without exceeding the digester's permissible load limits," explains Laug.
At the same time, substrate costs and expected gas production can be taken into account. The goal is not to produce as much gas as possible. What matters is when and how much gas is available, what it costs to produce, and how it can subsequently be used as effectively as possible.
Operators can already test a simulation tool on the institute's website that illustrates the effects of substrate mix and electricity prices on a biogas plant operating strategy optimized in line with electricity prices.
Applicable to other process engineering facilities
The principle underlying this data infrastructure can be applied to other process engineering facilities—from wastewater treatment plants to irrigation systems and drinking water supply systems. These facilities generate a large amount of measurement data and operational information, which are currently used primarily for real-time control.
In wastewater treatment plants, for example, typical opportunities for optimization include more demand-driven aeration of the biological treatment stage and the monitoring of energy-intensive equipment.
Existing facilities therefore do not need to be completely rebuilt to make better use of their data. Laug sums it up: "The first step toward a smart facility is to bring existing information together in a reliable, understandable data foundation. Forecasts, soft sensors and model-based operational optimization can then be built on that foundation."

candidato.titulo: Falhas críticas no PHP já eram exploradas por hackers antes de correção
candidato.resumo: As duas falhas críticas de segurança do PHP, que colocaram milhões de sites em alerta nesta semana, já eram alvo de tentativas de exploração por hackers desde 17 de outubro , quatro dias antes da divulgação das correções. A descoberta foi feita pela Amazon Web Services (AWS), que identificou atividades suspeitas em seus sistemas de monitoramento. Segundo informações divulgadas pela Wired nesta quinta-feira (22), os ataques começaram antes mesmo do vazamento de informações sobre as vulnerabilidades, ocorrido na terça-feira (20). A descoberta representa um novo desdobramento do alerta global de segurança provocado pelas falhas no PHP . As duas brechas, identificadas como CVE-2026-109618 e CVE-2026-109619, receberam classificação de gravidade de 9,2 em uma escala de 0 a 10. Apesar das tentativas registradas, ainda não há confirmação de invasões bem-sucedidas . À Wired, a PHP Foundation, organização que apoia o desenvolvimento da linguagem, afirmou não ter conhecimento de casos em que invasores conseguiram executar códigos maliciosos remotamente utilizando as vulnerabilidades. texto_fonte:
Falhas críticas no PHP já eram exploradas por hackers antes de correção
Por Marcelo Fischer |
As duas falhas críticas de segurança do PHP, que colocaram milhões de sites em alerta nesta semana, já eram alvo de tentativas de exploração por hackers desde 17 de outubro, quatro dias antes da divulgação das correções. A descoberta foi feita pela Amazon Web Services (AWS), que identificou atividades suspeitas em seus sistemas de monitoramento.
Segundo informações divulgadas pela Wired nesta quinta-feira (22), os ataques começaram antes mesmo do vazamento de informações sobre as vulnerabilidades, ocorrido na terça-feira (20).
A descoberta representa um novo desdobramento do alerta global de segurança provocado pelas falhas no PHP. As duas brechas, identificadas como CVE-2026-109618 e CVE-2026-109619, receberam classificação de gravidade de 9,2 em uma escala de 0 a 10.
Apesar das tentativas registradas, ainda não há confirmação de invasões bem-sucedidas. À Wired, a PHP Foundation, organização que apoia o desenvolvimento da linguagem, afirmou não ter conhecimento de casos em que invasores conseguiram executar códigos maliciosos remotamente utilizando as vulnerabilidades.
Como os hackers exploraram as falhas antes da correção?
A Amazon identificou os primeiros ataques ao analisar registros de sua rede MadPot, formada por servidores-isca, conhecidos como honeypots (potes de mel, em inglês).
Esses sistemas são utilizados para atrair tentativas de invasão e permitir que pesquisadores acompanhem as técnicas empregadas por criminosos.
O primeiro registro, de 17 de outubro, partiu de um endereço IP associado a um serviço comercial de anonimização, como uma rede de proxies ou VPN.
Segundo CJ Moses, diretor de segurança da AWS, a utilização desse tipo de infraestrutura para tentar explorar uma vulnerabilidade ainda mantida em sigilo indica uma possível atividade criminosa.
Entretanto, os pesquisadores não conseguiram determinar como o responsável pelo ataque obteve informações sobre a falha antes da divulgação pública.
A situação se intensificou em 21 de outubro. A Amazon identificou novas tentativas a partir das 2h UTC, equivalentes às 23h de terça-feira (20) no horário de Brasília, aproximadamente 12 horas antes da liberação das correções.
Nas seis horas seguintes, outros ataques partiram de diferentes serviços de anonimização e utilizaram códigos maliciosos distintos.
Para os pesquisadores, as diferenças sugerem a atuação de múltiplos grupos ou indivíduos, embora ainda não seja possível identificar os responsáveis.
Milhões de tentativas de invasão após divulgação das falhas
O número de ataques cresceu rapidamente depois que as vulnerabilidades se tornaram públicas.
Segundo Matthew Prince, CEO da Cloudflare, a empresa registrou milhares de tentativas de exploração nas dez horas anteriores à divulgação oficial.
O volume chegou a dezenas de milhares de tentativas nos primeiros 45 minutos após o anúncio e ultrapassou a marca de centenas de milhares em duas horas.
Ainda na quarta-feira (21), a quantidade acumulada de tentativas identificadas pela Cloudflare já havia chegado à casa dos milhões, conforme informações divulgadas pela Reuters.
A empresa também observou invasores modificando os códigos utilizados nos ataques para tentar contornar seus mecanismos de proteção.
Apesar do volume, é importante diferenciar tentativas de exploração de invasões efetivamente realizadas. Os números não significam que milhões de sites tenham sido comprometidos.
A Cloudflare afirma ter implementado proteções antes da divulgação oficial das vulnerabilidades, inclusive para clientes que utilizam seu serviço gratuito.
Essas medidas, porém, são temporárias e não substituem a atualização do PHP.
O que muda para quem já corrigiu as falhas?
A descoberta de ataques anteriores à divulgação pública exige que administradores de sites verifiquem se seus sistemas foram comprometidos antes da instalação das atualizações.
Segundo a Amazon, a recomendação é analisar registros de atividades suspeitas desde pelo menos 17 de outubro, e não apenas a partir de quarta-feira (21), quando as correções foram liberadas.
Entre os sinais que devem ser investigados estão requisições suspeitas enviadas aos servidores, execução inesperada de processos e alterações desconhecidas em arquivos.
A aplicação das correções impede a exploração das vulnerabilidades conhecidas, mas não desfaz eventuais alterações realizadas por invasores anteriormente.
A AWS também alerta que o avanço da inteligência artificial pode reduzir o intervalo entre a divulgação de uma falha e o desenvolvimento de ferramentas capazes de explorá-la.
Segundo a empresa, ferramentas de IA permitem analisar correções e identificar maneiras de contorná-las em questão de horas ou minutos. Entretanto, não há evidências de que os ataques identificados neste caso tenham utilizado inteligência artificial.
A descoberta reforça a preocupação com a segurança do PHP, linguagem utilizada por quase 70% dos sites cuja tecnologia de servidor é conhecida.
Até o momento, as empresas responsáveis pelo monitoramento não divulgaram um número confirmado de sites efetivamente invadidos por meio das duas vulnerabilidades.
